summary: This document defines how versions of the NFS protocol bind to RPC-over-RDMA version 1, which enables direct data placement so data can move straight between memory without extra copying. It obsoletes RFC 5667.

eli5.summary: It lets a file server drop data straight into the right spot in a computer's memory, like a delivery driver putting a package right in your room.

questions: nfs upper layer binding for rpc-over-rdma
what is an upper layer binding
which port does nfs over rdma use
what data can nfs place directly in memory
subtitle: The agreement that tells NFS clients and servers which data may be placed directly into memory over RPC-over-RDMA.

tldr.problem: RPC-over-RDMA version 1 can place data payloads directly into the receiver's memory, but a client and server must agree in advance which NFS data items and procedures are eligible.
tldr.mechanism: This Upper-Layer Binding lists the DDP-eligible items for NFS versions 2, 3, 4.0, 4.1 and 4.2, explains how to estimate reply sizes, how to pair Write chunks with results, and which port to use.
tldr.outcome: It obsoletes RFC 5667 and covers NFS version 4 minor versions up to 4.2. Later NFS version 4 changes would need IETF standards action to extend the binding.

today: RFC 8267 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 5667. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: What an Upper-Layer Binding Does
sections.content:
RPC-over-RDMA version 1 can use Direct Data Placement (DDP) to carry data payloads of RPC transactions (RFC 8166). For this to work, client and server must agree which External Data Representation (XDR) data items and RPC procedures are DDP-eligible.

An Upper-Layer Binding records that agreement for one or more versions of one RPC program. It also covers operational details such as RPC binding assignments, pairing Write chunks with result data items, and reply size estimation.

This document supplies the binding for NFS versions 2, 3, 4.0, 4.1 and 4.2, plus the auxiliary protocols used with NFS versions 2 and 3. It assumes the reader knows the terminology of RFC 8166.
sections.eli5: When two computers want to hand data straight into memory, they first need to agree which pieces of data are allowed to travel that way. This document writes that agreement down for NFS.

sections.title: Reply Size Estimation
sections.content:
When building an RPC Call, the requester must set aside resources for the Reply. If the Reply may be larger than the inline threshold, it provides Write and/or Reply chunks where the responder can put results. A reply resource overrun happens when the Reply does not fit, which stops the responder from returning the reply at all.

Usually the NFS XDR definition lets a client predict the maximum size. It can do so when it asks for only part of an object (the count and offset of a READ), limits the number of results (the count of READDIR), already knows the object's size from an earlier GETATTR, or has negotiated a maximum size with the server, for example through CREATE_SESSION.

In a few cases the size cannot be known. If the server finds the client's buffers too small, it returns an RPC-level or transport error such as ERR_CHUNK. The client may then give up, or send the same request again as a new transaction with a larger Reply chunk and a new XID. This short Reply chunk retry should be used only where the RFC says so; otherwise underestimating is an implementation bug.
sections.eli5: Before asking for a delivery, you have to prepare a box big enough for it. Usually you can guess the size. If the box turns out too small, you may try again with a bigger one.

sections.title: Binding for NFS Versions 2 and 3
sections.content:
For NFS versions 2 and 3 (the "Legacy" versions), only four XDR data items are DDP-eligible: the opaque file data in WRITE, the pathname in SYMLINK, the opaque file data result in READ, and the pathname result in READLINK. Everything else is not eligible. No operation in these versions benefits from short Reply chunk retry.

Legacy servers traditionally listen on UDP and TCP port 2049 and register with a portmapper. A Legacy server supporting RPC-over-RDMA version 1 MAY choose an arbitrary port or use the alternative well-known port, and MAY register it with the portmapper.

For the auxiliary protocols, MOUNT, NLM and NSM have historically been carried over TCP, so a Legacy server MUST support them over TCP. NFSACL has no DDP-eligible items because ACLs are typically small. Since an ACL's size cannot be known in advance, a client may use short Reply chunk retry when a GETACL hits a transport error.
sections.eli5: For the older versions of NFS, only file contents and link paths may be dropped straight into memory. Everything else goes the ordinary way.

sections.title: Binding for NFS Version 4
sections.content:
For all NFS version 4 minor versions, only four items in the COMPOUND procedure are DDP-eligible: the opaque data in WRITE4args, the linkdata of the NF4LNK arm in createtype4, the opaque data in READ4resok, and the linkdata in READLINK4resok.

Reply sizes. Some version 4 results have no protocol size limit, such as attrlist4, ACL fields, fs_locations4 and pNFS layout metadata. For minor version 0 a client may use short Reply chunk retry for a COMPOUND containing GETATTR, and should send a GETATTR with unpredictable result length in a COMPOUND by itself so it is not combined with a non-idempotent operation such as RENAME. For minor version 1 and later, the ca_maxresponsesize value from CREATE_SESSION is the absolute maximum reply size.

Port. A version 4 server using RPC-over-RDMA version 1 MUST use the alternative well-known port. Clients SHOULD connect to it without consulting the portmapper.

Several DDP items in one COMPOUND. The first Write chunk is used by the first READ operation, the next chunk by the next, and so on. A non-empty matching chunk MUST be used for the data item. An empty matching chunk means that operation MUST return its results inline. If a READ returns a union arm with no DDP-eligible result, the server MUST return an empty Write chunk in that position. READ operations without a matching chunk MUST return inline.

Chunk list complexity. Without knowledge of the server's limits, clients SHOULD use a Read list with a Position Zero Read chunk, one Read chunk with a non-zero Position, or both; a Write list with at most one Write chunk; and no more than sixteen RDMA segments per chunk. Servers MUST accept such requests. A server that cannot process a request answers with an ERR_CHUNK RDMA_ERROR or an RPC Reply with GARBAGE_ARGS, and the client SHOULD NOT retransmit.
sections.eli5: For NFS version 4 the same four kinds of items can travel directly. When a request contains several reads, the first prepared box is for the first read, the second box for the second, and so on. An empty box means send that answer the normal way.

sections.title: Callbacks, Sessions and Transport
sections.content:
Callbacks. NFS version 4.0 typically uses a separate TCP connection for callbacks, and none of its callback items are DDP-eligible. For version 4.1 and newer, clients and servers MUST use the approach in RFC 8167 when callbacks share an RPC-over-RDMA connection. There are no DDP-eligible items in version 4.1 or 4.2 callbacks, though large callbacks may need a Long Call or Reply.

Sessions. NFS sessions have no effect on RPC-over-RDMA version 1, and there is no need to match session slots to RPC-over-RDMA credits. When a transport error such as RDMA_ERROR ends a transaction, the requester's session code performs slot recovery so the slot is not lost.

Congestion and keep-alive. RDMA Reliable Connections are reliable and in-order, so they meet the congestion-avoidance requirements RFC 7530 and RFC 5661 place on NFS version 4 transports. Some RDMA transports have no keep-alive, so a client could wait forever once its credits are used up. Clients SHOULD therefore reserve one RPC-over-RDMA credit for periodic health checks of the server or connection.
sections.eli5: The rules also say how to cope when a message goes missing, and to keep one spare ticket for a quick check that the other side is still awake.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: RPC-over-RDMA version 1 supports all RPC security models, including RPCSEC_GSS and transport-level security (RFC 7861). Choosing a Direct Data Placement mechanism changes only how data is transferred, so it does not affect this. Because the document defines only the binding of NFS atop RFC 8166, the relevant security considerations are described at that layer.
sections.eli5: Moving data straight into memory does not change who is allowed to ask for it. The same locks and keys still apply.

sections.title: Port Assignment
sections.content:
Networks that share the traditional UDP and TCP port spaces with RDMA services, such as iWARP, need an extra port number for NFS. IANA has assigned nfsrdma port 20049 for TCP, UDP and SCTP, with this document as the reference.

Section 7 adds that the binding can be extended, through IETF standards action, to NFS version 4 minor versions defined after 4.2 or to separately published extensions to an existing minor version as described in RFC 8178.
sections.eli5: NFS over this fast path gets its own door number, 20049, so it does not mix with the usual NFS door.
